sources.title: Pedro Álvares Cabral (Q174432), verified live via the Wikidata API (2026-11-24): English label 'Pedro Álvares Cabral', description 'Portuguese military commander and explorer (c.1467/8 - c.1521)', human, birth 1467 and death 1520 (year precision), citizenship Kingdom of Portugal, Korean label 페드루 알바르스 카브랄 (same as the Korean Wikipedia title). Orientation only; not used as support for any row.

Pedro Calmon, 'Pedro Álvares Cabral', Encyclopaedia Britannica (editors' article read in full). CANONICAL SIGNIFICANCE SOURCE: Portuguese navigator generally credited as the first European to reach Brazil on 22 April 1500 (Vicente Yáñez Pinzón may have reached it slightly earlier); King Manuel I gave him command of the 13-ship fleet that left Lisbon on 9 March 1500, the second European expedition to India round the Cape of Good Hope; four ships were lost with all hands on 29 May; he reached Calicut on 13 September 1500, set up a fortified trading post, and after the post was attacked on 17 December bombarded the city and took ten Muslim vessels; he loaded spices at Cochin and Cannanore and reached the Tagus on 23 June 1501 with four ships; passed over for the next command, he held no further post. Short reference article; accounts differ on why the king chose da Gama instead.

Francis A. Dutra, 'Cabral, Pedro Álvares (1468-c. 1520)', Encyclopedia of Latin American History and Culture (Gale, reproduced on Encyclopedia.com; read in full with its bibliography). Reference entry: the 1500 fleet of thirteen ships; first recorded Portuguese sighting of Brazil on 22 April 1500; friendly relations with the inhabitants at Porto Seguro and two Masses; a supply ship sent to King Manuel with the surviving letters of Pero Vaz de Caminha and Mestre João Faras; the bombardment of Calicut and friendly relations with Cochin. States that relatively little is known about the man himself and that most scholars now believe he was unaware of Brazil until winds and currents brought land into view. Limits the profile: evidence concerns the voyage, not the person's life.

William Brooks Greenlee, introduction ('The Voyage') to The Voyage of Pedro Alvares Cabral to Brazil and India from Contemporary Documents and Narratives (Hakluyt Society, London, 1938; Internet Archive scan of the Central Archaeological Library copy, introduction read in full). Scholarly synthesis built on the eyewitness texts: the choice of Cabral, the westward course after the Cape Verde Islands, the ten days at Porto Seguro, the storm of 24 May that sank four ships and scattered the fleet, the regrouping at Mozambique, the Kilwa and Malindi calls, the weeks of haggling over hostages at Calicut, the storming of the factory in which all but about twenty of seventy men were killed or captured, Cabral's wait of a day for an apology, the seizure of ten Arab ships and a day's bombardment of Calicut, the alliance with Cochin and the homeward voyage. Greenlee says the Portuguese carried instructions to seize Arab ships, that Cabral's manner at Calicut seemed unnecessarily belligerent and condescending, and that the truth of the massacre will never be known. Independent modern scholarly voice, though it rests on the same Portuguese eyewitness and chronicle record.

Pero Vaz de Caminha, letter to King Manuel from Porto Seguro, 1 May 1500, as translated and introduced by W. B. Greenlee in The Voyage of Pedro Alvares Cabral (Hakluyt Society, 1938; read in full). Contemporary eyewitness account by a clerk of the fleet, the first document on the landfall in Brazil: records Cabral's actions day by day, including receiving two local men aboard with gifts and bedding, ordering the first Mass on 26 April, consulting all the captains on whether to send news to the king by the supply ship, the decision to leave two convicts, and the raising of the cross. Subordinate's report to the king (so it may flatter the commander) and it covers only the Brazil stay.

The Anonymous Narrative of the voyage of Cabral ('Navigatione de Lisbona a Callichut', published in Paesi novamente retrovati, Vicenza, 1507), translated in Greenlee's Hakluyt Society volume (1938; read through the Calicut episode). Contemporary account by an unknown Portuguese member of the fleet who was ashore at Calicut and survived the factory massacre: Cabral's council with his officers over the present for the king of Malindi, his returning the captured ships of the Malindi king's cousin with honour, the long negotiations over hostages, the reception by the Zamorin; Greenlee ranks it second only to the Caminha and Master John letters. Eyewitness, anonymous and possibly an official record; editorial notes quote a Persian chronicle of Kilwa that tells the Kilwa visit differently.

K. M. Panikkar, Malabar and the Portuguese: Being a History of the Relations of the Portuguese with Malabar from 1500 to 1663 (Bombay, 1929), chapter on da Gama and Cabral (read). COUNTER-VOICE from the Malabar side, drawing on Portuguese chroniclers and Kerala tradition: calls Cabral untactful, proud and short-tempered, blames his seizure of Arab ships for provoking the attack on the factory, describes the retaliation as brutal and says he fled when the Zamorin's fleet approached Cochin. A polemical 1929 history that contains errors (it gives 33 ships and 1,500 men) and differs from Greenlee on the Cochin departure; used only as a contrasting reading.

collaboration.rationale: [src_cabral_caminha, src_cabral_anon, src_cabral_greenlee | 1500 | contemporary eyewitness letter, anonymous eyewitness narrative, scholarly synthesis] At Porto Seguro all the captains came to the flagship and he asked whether to send news to the king by the supply ship and whether to leave convicts ashore, and at Malindi the narrative says it was agreed in council who should carry the royal present ashore. Two separate eyewitness texts describe consultation, but royal instructions may have required it and both were written by subordinates. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.50 strong_inference to 58 / 0.44 inference.

decisiveness.rationale: [src_cabral_greenlee, src_cabral_britannica, src_cabral_panikkar | 1500 | scholarly synthesis, reference article, polemical history] After the factory was stormed he waited a day for an apology and then seized ten Arab ships and bombarded Calicut, and on learning of the Zamorin's large fleet at Cochin he left for Portugal at once (Greenlee says on second thought, Panikkar that his nerve failed). The two historians read the same departure in opposite ways, so the row stays near the middle. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 58 / 0.44 to 56 / 0.40.

conflict_tolerance.rationale: [src_cabral_greenlee, src_cabral_anon, src_cabral_panikkar | 1500 | scholarly synthesis, eyewitness narrative, polemical history] Greenlee finds his manner at Calicut unnecessarily belligerent and condescending, and Panikkar calls him proud and short-tempered; the reprisal after the factory was stormed was severe. Against this, he carried instructions to seize Arab ships, the narrative has him returning the ships of the Malindi king's cousin with honour, and Greenlee notes that the long hostage haggling followed his orders, so the behaviour cannot be separated from policy. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 64 / 0.42 to 60 / 0.38 for orders-versus-character confusion and a polemical source.

persistence.rationale: [src_cabral_greenlee, src_cabral_anon, src_cabral_britannica | 1500-1501 | scholarly synthesis, eyewitness narrative, reference article] After a sudden storm on 24 May sank four of thirteen ships and scattered the rest, his ship and two others pressed on round the Cape, regrouped with some of the others at Mozambique, repaired for ten days and reached Calicut and Cochin, then sailed home with the surviving ships carrying spices (Britannica counts four ships at the Tagus; Greenlee lists five arrivals in July 1501 plus the Anunciada in June). Continuing the royal mission is documented; how much was his own resolve and how much the instructions is not. SELF-CALIBRATION (agent): lowered from 62 / 0.44 to 58 / 0.40.

portrait.source: Engraved portrait plate of Pedro Alvares Cabral, signed 'Cunha delin.' (drawn) and 'Abrantes grav.' (engraved) and inscribed 'Pedro Alvares Cabral, Senhor de Belmonte, Alcaide mor d'Azurara, Descobridor do Brazil', printed in Pedro Jose de Figueiredo, Retratos, e elogios dos varoes, e donas, que illustraram a nacao portugueza, vol. 1 (Lisboa: Na officina de Simao Thaddeo Ferreira, 1817), the plate facing the Cabral sketch that begins on printed page 15; scan of the Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library, University of Toronto copy at the Internet Archive (retratoseelogios01figu, leaf n347, 500 ppi). The file is the plate cropped from the 2490 x 3811 page image and downscaled to 642 x 1000 with no upscaling.
portrait.license: Public domain by age: engraved and published in Lisbon in 1817; the draughtsman and engraver (Cunha and Abrantes) were working in or before 1817, so no copyright term of life plus 70 years can still run in Portugal, and the work was published before 1931 in the United States. The Internet Archive record carries no rights statement of its own; the University of Toronto Libraries' reuse page and the Internet Archive terms could not be opened (404 and script wall), so no holder policy is claimed
portrait.attribution: LATER DEPICTION, NOT A LIFETIME LIKENESS: engraving published in 1817, about 300 years after the sitter's death, by Abrantes after a drawing by Cunha (names as signed on the plate). From Retratos, e elogios dos varoes, e donas, que illustraram a nacao portugueza, vol. 1 (Lisboa, 1817); Internet Archive scan of the University of Toronto, Thomas Fisher Rare Book Library copy; cropped and downscaled.
portrait.creator: Abrantes (engraver) after Cunha (draughtsman), as signed on the plate
